explain.say: The Leaning Tower of Pisa began to tilt while it was still being built, in the twelfth century, because the soft clay under one side squeezed more than under the other. That slow squeezing is consolidation. On the board, a new building adds forty kilopascals on top of a four metre layer of soft clay between two sand layers.

explain.say: Think of the clay as a sponge full of water. When the load arrives, the water in its tiny pores carries it at first. Clay lets water through very slowly, so it can only seep out bit by bit into the sand above and below. As it leaves, the grains take over the load and the layer gets thinner. Why does sand settle quickly instead?

explain.say: Its water escapes at once! How much will our clay settle? We use the compression index from a lab test, zero point three, with an initial void ratio of one and an existing effective stress of eighty kilopascals. Adding forty kilopascals gives about a hundred and six millimetres of settlement.

explain.say: And how long? Look at the curve. Settlement is quick at first, then slows right down. With drainage at both faces, half of it, fifty three millimetres, takes about five months, and ninety percent takes about one point seven years. Time grows with the square of the drainage path, so a thicker layer takes far longer.

draw.text: Drainage path d = 2 m (half the layer); c_v = 2 m² per year.

explain.say: Engineers speed this up by preloading the ground with a mound of earth and by installing vertical drains, which shorten the path the water must travel. Kansai Airport in Japan, on an artificial island over soft seabed clay, has settled many metres and is watched closely. Wonderful! Challenge: if the clay drained only at the top, how would the time change?

faq.a: Consolidation is the slow compression of a saturated clay as water is squeezed out of its pores under a new load, while the grains take over the load. It can go on for years.
asks: Why do buildings on clay settle?

faq.q: Why does clay settle slowly but sand quickly?
faq.a: Sand has high permeability, so its pore water escapes almost instantly. Clay's permeability can be millions of times lower, so the water takes months or years to drain.

faq.q: How do you calculate consolidation settlement?
faq.a: For a normally consolidated clay, settlement equals C c times H over 1 plus e nought, times the log of final over initial effective stress. Here that gives about 106 millimetres.
Time equals the time factor T v times the drainage path squared, divided by the coefficient of consolidation. For 90 percent, T v is about 0.848, giving about 1.7 years for our layer.

faq.q: How can consolidation be speeded up?
faq.a: By preloading the site with a temporary mound of earth and by installing vertical drains, such as sand drains or plastic wick drains, which shorten the drainage path.

facts: Consolidation time grows with the square of the drainage path: t = T_v d²/c_v, with T_v ≈ 0.848 for 90 percent consolidation.
Karl Terzaghi developed the one-dimensional theory of consolidation in the 1920s.

quiz.say: A clay layer takes 2 years to reach 90 percent consolidation. If its drainage path doubles, how long will it take?
quiz.show: A clay layer takes 2 years to reach 90% consolidation. If its drainage path doubles, it takes…
quiz.why: Time grows with the drainage path squared: 2² = 4, and 4 × 2 years = 8 years.

wrong.0: That assumes time grows in direct proportion to the path.
wrong.2: A longer path always slows drainage down.
